Oh that's a good question, let me think. So there are honestly a lot of examples I could pick from because my last team was kind of chaotic, we had three reorgs in one year, which, you know, is a whole story in itself. But I guess the one that comes to mind is when we were building this internal tool for the support team, it was like a dashboard slash workflow thing, and the requirements kept changing because the support org itself kept changing, like the manager who asked for it left halfway through, and the new manager had totally different ideas, and also the data team was migrating the warehouse at the same time so our data sources kept breaking. So it was a mess. Anyway I was the main engineer on it, well, me and one other person, and we just kind of kept going, we talked to the new manager, re-scoped some stuff, cut some features, and eventually shipped a version people actually used. I think support handle time went down, they told us it helped anyway. It took way longer than planned though, like five months instead of two.

Right, so specifically what I did — when the new manager came in, I set up a meeting where instead of showing him the old requirements doc I showed him the actual half-built tool and asked him to walk through a real support ticket using it. That surfaced that like half of what we'd built didn't match how his team actually worked. So I cut those features, which was painful because it was my code, and re-scoped to just the ticket triage flow. I also started sending a weekly one-paragraph update to him and my manager so nobody would be surprised again. The data source breakage I mostly just handled reactively, I'll admit, I didn't have a great system for that.

Handle time, yeah, so the support ops person tracked it, I think it was around 15% faster on triage after two months, though honestly some of that was probably their new hires ramping up at the same time, it's hard to fully attribute. I should have set up a cleaner baseline before launch, that's fair.

Conflict, hmm, okay so this one is a bit awkward but there was a senior engineer on a sister team who kept blocking my PRs on our shared library, like every review would be twenty comments about style and architecture philosophy, and it was adding like a week to every change. And some of his points were right, to be fair, the library was genuinely inconsistent because so many teams touched it. But it was killing my velocity. So eventually I asked him to pair with me on the next change instead of reviewing async, and honestly that one session changed a lot, because half the comments turned out to be him not having context on why my team needed the thing at all, and once he had it he was way more flexible. We ended up co-writing a style doc for the library so the rules were explicit instead of living in his head. Reviews went from a week to like a day or two after that.

I mean, the thing I changed on my side was I stopped treating his reviews as obstruction. Once we paired I realized I'd been writing PR descriptions that assumed context nobody outside my team had. So now I write the why section first, before the what. That habit stuck.

A failure, okay. So the honest one is I once sat on a flaky test for like two months. It was in our payments integration suite, it failed maybe one run in ten, and I kept retrying it and moving on because I was heads down on a feature deadline, and I sort of assumed it was infra flakiness because our CI was genuinely flaky at the time. Turns out it was a real race condition, and it eventually hit in production during a traffic spike, duplicate payment attempts for I think a few hundred users, most got caught by the idempotency layer but around 40 customers got double-charged and support had to refund them manually. The postmortem was uncomfortable because the timeline showed the test had been warning us for two months and my retry-and-move-on pattern was right there in the CI history. What I did after was I proposed a rule that a test that fails more than twice a week gets quarantined with a ticket and an owner, so flakiness becomes visible work instead of background noise. The team still uses that.

In the moment, the day it hit production, I was actually the one who connected it to the flaky test because I recognized the stack trace, so I flagged it in the incident channel, and that shortcut the diagnosis by probably a few hours. Which doesn't undo sitting on it for two months, but it's why the fix went out same-day.

What would I do differently — I mean beyond the quarantine rule, the real lesson for me was about deadline tunnel vision, like the feature I was rushing ended up slipping a week anyway for unrelated reasons, so the time I saved ignoring the test was fake savings. I try to remember that math now when I'm tempted to skip something that smells wrong.
